title: Seven Deadly Fitness Sins: Sloth
summary: First of a seven-part series mapping the seven deadly sins onto lifting. Sloth is skipping training when you merely don't feel like it, and, for experienced lifters, complacency: no longer pushing or respecting progressive overload, then blaming a 'natural limit'.

claims.claim: He is an avid reader and frames the seven deadly sins, a recurring literary theme, as things lifters must avoid to achieve their best physique.
Sloth is the unwillingness to do something you know you should do, not because you can't but because you don't feel like it; even passionate lifters have days without the fire.
Most non-lifters would take a pill that replicates training; they want the body but not the work, which is laziness.
TV and video games are fine in themselves, but there is such a thing as too much time spent on non-productive activities.
Skipping one session every two weeks adds up over a year to a lot of missed sets, reps and tonnage, which is progress you never made.
Skipping because you have to is different: job, studies, family and loved ones come before the gym, but the gym comes right after; if he has nothing else on, he trains.
Sloth also means no longer pushing yourself; the number one reason long-term lifters he knows stopped progressing is that they stopped making training hard.
Stalled lifters either never had a progressive overload scheme or stopped respecting it, then claimed a natural limit; the only limit they reached was their willingness to work.

Complacency is a form of sloth: even training daily and dieting strictly, you are lazy if you are comfortable and no longer pushing, and by the standard you apply to non-lifters you would be called lazy.
The more work you put in, as long as it is smart and within a progressive overload scheme, the more results you get.
